items.questionAndWhy: Can merely imagining contact with an object associated with a moral or immoral peer change adolescents’ stated willingness to help?
items.whatTheyDid: In a class-based guided-imagery experiment, 207 seventh-grade students from six intact classes imagined wearing a glove associated with a morally positive, morally negative, or neutral peer. Researchers measured self-reported prosocial tendencies, moral elevation, and Junzi personality.
items.whatTheyFound: Self-reported prosocial scores were highest in the positive-cue condition, then the negative and neutral conditions. A statistical indirect effect through moral elevation appeared for positive cues, not negative ones. Only two classes entered each condition, and outcomes were post-task self-reports rather than observed helping.
items.whatItMeans: Symbolic associations can change immediate moral self-assessments in this setting, but class-level assignment and simultaneous mediator/outcome measures prevent strong claims about mechanisms. For PSYWERX this suggests a bounded hypothesis about moral cues and social identity, not evidence that online moral messaging causes prosocial action.
items.streamTitle: Imagined contact with moral exemplars shifted adolescents’ reported prosocial tendencies
items.streamSummary: A six-class, 207-student guided-imagery experiment linked imagined contact with positive moral exemplars to higher self-reported prosociality. The outcome was not actual helping, and statistical mediation did not prove a mechanism.
items.attribution: Li and Yang — Scientific Reports (class-based guided-imagery experiment)

items.questionAndWhy: When people learn that an admired creator committed a moral transgression, do they reconstruct how they remember feeling about the person and the creation differently?
items.whatTheyDid: Across five preregistered experiments, researchers presented negative revelations about creators and compared retrospective evaluations of those creators and their art. Tests included previously held and experimentally induced positive evaluations, multiple creative domains, and designs intended to limit demand and recall artifacts.
items.whatTheyFound: Participants revised memories of their past appreciation for the creator downward while memories of their prior enjoyment of the work remained comparatively protected. This is evidence about retrospective ratings under the tested conditions, not evidence that all autobiographical memories are rewritten or that later behavior changes.
items.whatItMeans: This distinction suggests that source reputation and message-content evaluation need not move together when new moral information arrives. For PSYWERX, the relevance is an experimentally testable separation between judgments of a communicator and retrospective evaluations of their material; generalization to political information remains untested.
items.streamTitle: New revelations reshaped remembered opinions of creators more than their work
items.streamSummary: Five preregistered experiments found that negative revelations changed recollections of liking an artist more than recollections of liking the art. The result concerns retrospective judgments, not verified changes in past experience.
items.attribution: Shin, Rozin and Zauberman — Journal of Experimental Social Psychology (five preregistered experiments)

items.questionAndWhy: How do students’ beliefs about their AI competence, AI literacy, AI acceptance, and AI anxiety relate to one another?
items.whatTheyDid: A cross-sectional survey of 622 undergraduates at one Turkish public university measured AI self-efficacy, literacy, acceptance and anxiety through questionnaires, then used correlations and regression-based mediation models.
items.whatTheyFound: AI self-efficacy was positively associated with acceptance directly and through measured literacy; higher acceptance correlated with lower AI anxiety. No variable was experimentally assigned, and the statistical pathways cannot establish whether literacy caused acceptance or acceptance reduced anxiety.
items.whatItMeans: Practitioner education can distinguish confidence, demonstrated literacy, willingness to use tools, and anxiety instead of treating adoption as a single outcome. Testing whether instruction changes subsequent AI use or competence requires randomized or longitudinal evaluation, not just survey mediation.
items.streamTitle: AI confidence and literacy correlated with acceptance and lower anxiety in students
items.streamSummary: A 622-student Turkish survey linked AI confidence and literacy to acceptance, and acceptance to lower anxiety. The reported mediated pathways are correlational, not evidence that literacy training caused adoption.
items.attribution: İşbulan et al. — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (cross-sectional survey)

items.questionAndWhy: What observable account histories and network behavior link apparent American-voter personas to an established inauthentic influence operation before the 2026 U.S. midterms?
items.whatTheyDid: Graphika’s October 30 original investigation compared X account histories, interactions, language artifacts and reposting behavior. It identified three activity sets: a successor account, four historical Spamouflage accounts amplifying a conservative persona, and a repurposed Philippine-culture account.
items.whatTheyFound: The investigators found cross-partisan divisive election narratives, signs of prior Spamouflage involvement, and amplification often confined to network accounts. The repurposed account exceeded 200,000 followers, but whether it was sold, hijacked or otherwise transferred is unresolved; reach, persuasion and voting effects were not established.
items.whatItMeans: Attribution should combine account history, coordination and content rather than infer state control from a single linguistic cue. Information-environment assessment should measure authentic audience uptake separately from inauthentic amplification and follower counts. This is investigator attribution, not experimentally demonstrated election influence.
items.streamTitle: Graphika traced renewed Spamouflage-linked election personas and mostly closed amplification
items.streamSummary: Graphika documented three Spamouflage-linked activity sets using voter personas, repurposed accounts and mostly in-network amplification. Attribution and audience reach are bounded; no voter effect was measured.
items.attribution: Graphika Research Team — The #Americans: Season 2 (original network investigation, October 30)

items.questionAndWhy: Can an apparently independent network of political news sites seed sources cited by conversational search tools in low-information elections?
items.whatTheyDid: VisionHeight’s October 7 investigation examined registration data, site templates, crawler access rules and repeated candidate language across 37 purported local-news or opinion websites. In October 30 follow-up testing, NPR queried ChatGPT about targeted congressional races and checked its citations.
items.whatTheyFound: VisionHeight reported 36 of 37 domains registered within eight minutes, long candidate Q&A pages and more than 360 repetitions of a candidate-favoring phrase. NPR found a network site cited in 19 tested answers, approximately half its prompts; those tests do not establish voter persuasion, and the operator remains unidentified.
items.whatItMeans: This is a concrete source-laundering risk for AI-assisted information searches: apparently independent citations may share one operator. Audits should trace domain registration, editorial identity, interlinkage and retrieval outputs, without assuming that citation frequency proves electoral effects. The primary investigation predates today but gained independent relevance from the October 30 follow-up.
items.streamTitle: Coordinated fake-local-news sites reached chatbot citations in election queries
items.streamSummary: VisionHeight documented 37 coordinated election-information sites designed for machine retrieval; NPR later observed their citations in 19 ChatGPT responses. The operator and effects on voters remain unknown.
items.attribution: VisionHeight — VH-2026-035 original investigation (October 7), with NPR follow-up (October 30)

items.questionAndWhy: Do agent systems that solve individual coding tasks reliably also complete streams of tasks arriving under shared CPU and memory constraints?
items.whatTheyDid: AOS-Bench ran independently verified tasks as both isolated jobs and 10-task or 20-task workloads on a shared four-CPU, eight-gigabyte workspace. Five model–harness pairs were compared under different task-intake and concurrency policies.
items.whatTheyFound: All five systems lost about 13–23 percentage points of task success under heavy workloads. Two systems separated by only 0.6 points in isolation delivered roughly 54% versus 68% of medium-stream tasks. Serial dispatch left 73% of heavy tasks unclaimed, while fixed concurrency of two approached the best adaptive policy.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX automation, single-task benchmark scores are inadequate evidence of dependable multi-job research operations. Verify complete deliverables, unclaimed work, resource contention and final artifacts across concurrent workloads. These were coding/computer tasks, not experiments about human behavioral modeling.
items.streamTitle: Agent workload benchmark exposed large drops from isolated to concurrent task delivery
items.streamSummary: AOS-Bench compared five agent configurations on isolated versus shared workloads and found heavy-load success fell 13–23 points. Intake and concurrency policy mattered; agent self-reported completion was not the scoring criterion.
items.attribution: Zhu et al. — arXiv preprint (AOS-Bench verified agent evaluation)

items.questionAndWhy: How does showing collective popularity information change recommendation dynamics in populations of interacting language-model agents?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers replicated the structure of a classic Music Lab social-influence experiment with large populations of LLM agents recommending unfamiliar songs, comparing conditions with and without visible cumulative recommendation counts.
items.whatTheyFound: Exposing agents to prior recommendation totals produced extreme, unpredictable cascades increasingly detached from estimated intrinsic song appeal. The authors report stronger herding and less self-correction than in human comparison results; the new experimental subjects were LLM agents, not a newly randomized human population.
items.whatItMeans: Synthetic societies can generate social dynamics that look plausible but diverge quantitatively from human patterns. For PSYWERX, popularity feedback should be a sensitivity variable, and simulated cascades must be compared with human observations before forecasting real audience behavior.
items.streamTitle: LLM collectives showed exaggerated recommendation herding and unstable cascades
items.streamSummary: A Music Lab-style experiment found LLM-agent populations herded strongly when shown popularity counts, with more extreme and less self-correcting cascades than human comparators. It is AI-agent evidence, not human-field validation.
items.attribution: Hashemi et al. — arXiv preprint (LLM-agent social-influence simulations)

items.questionAndWhy: Can explicit decision rules in a generative model reveal how historical infrastructure choices balanced terrain with political or economic objectives?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers constructed a hierarchical generative inference model that simulated route choices using road straightness and slope-gradient trade-offs, then fitted it to 62 documented Roman roads in modern Wales.
items.whatTheyFound: Estimated trade-offs varied substantially across the 62 routes; no single straightness-versus-slope rule explained all road construction. The authors interpret heterogeneity in light of political and economic motivations, but these motivations were inferred from observed routes rather than documented decisions or experimental manipulations.
items.whatItMeans: The transferable advance is fitting competing behavioral decision rules to observed choices rather than assuming one rule for every actor. Applying analogous inverse inference to modern social or operational decisions is an untested methodological hypothesis, and fitted preferences may be confounded by omitted constraints.
items.streamTitle: Generative road-choice inference found no single rule across 62 Roman routes
items.streamSummary: A hierarchical generative model fit to 62 Roman roads found heterogeneous terrain-versus-directness trade-offs. The inferred motivations are model interpretations; transfer to present-day decision modeling remains untested.
items.attribution: Lewis and Crema — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (generative historical decision modeling)

items.questionAndWhy: Can an external eye tracker provide comparable, reproducible gaze measurements across mixed- and augmented-reality headsets with different software systems?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers created an open-source mounting, calibration and processing framework around Pupil Labs Neon and evaluated it on Meta Quest 3, Apple Vision Pro and XREAL Air 2 Ultra. They compared fixation accuracy and precision with the existing NeonXR method.
items.whatTheyFound: Mean Quest 3 angular error improved from 2.281° with NeonXR to 1.727° in the proposed pipeline; reported means were 1.324° on Vision Pro and 1.835° on XREAL. Calibration was tested on controlled targets at a fixed depth, not unrestricted real-world interaction or device refitting.
items.whatItMeans: The enabling capability is reusable gaze measurement across distinct XR platforms, supporting attention and interaction experiments without locking an entire workflow to one headset ecosystem. Behavioral validity, 3D depth sensitivity and robustness during natural movement still require task-specific evaluation. This May study is included for direct tooling relevance.
items.streamTitle: OpenEye measured cross-headset gaze tracking with a reproducible calibration toolkit
items.streamSummary: An open-source external eye-tracking toolkit improved Quest 3 gaze error from 2.281° to 1.727° and was tested on two additional headsets. Accuracy was measured in controlled tasks, not naturalistic attention studies.
items.attribution: Park, Han and Oakley — Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (cross-device toolkit evaluation)
